scenario: AITA for wanting my girlfriend to be less braggy about her work perks? She seems to forget that the way she lives isn't how most people live... | My girlfriend has a pretty sweet job. She doesn't have set hours; she just has to work 35 hours a week whenever is convenient for her and make it to her few meetings. She can work from the office or from home sometimes. She has a full benefits package despite being under what most people consider full time. A really nice retirement package too. And the company will pay everything for continued education. She does work she finds interesting (cutting edge robotics) and gets along well with her coworkers. She has a lot of PTO per year and her boss even lets the employees "earn up" more; if they work extra hours one week they can ask for the equivalent in PTO for later. Her team's managers buy them whatever they want for the office; they want a 500 dollar expresso maker, they get it. They want a type of fancy coffee, they get it. Nice furniture, done... They get paid well too; pretty middle of the road salary for robotics but she says the work life balance more than makes up for it. She'd rather have more time than be a top earner. And honestly a midrange robotics salary is still damn good. And anyway, For a while I thought "good for her" for having found something that she is happy with. But recently it's gotten frustrating because I think she forgets that this isn't how everyone lives. Like when we're out with my friends or just hanging out she'll talk about the nice stuff her managers bought for the office, about all the vacations she takes, about how she and her coworkers left the office in the middle of the day to see a movie then came back and just worked a little later. And yeah, it seems like she forgets that is no way a normal job. So last night we were at a party and she mentioned how she was going to tour a few new apartments Monday morning and afternoon, and one of the people at the party was like "don't you have work" and she said "yeah but I can set my own hours" And that just rubbed me the wrong way and I said that she needed to stop going on and on about her work perks, it was obnoxious and came off braggy. She was like "I was just explaining something" and I said it wasn't just this, it was everything. Most people don't live the life she lives." She said that I was coming off jealous and that it was a bad look. That she was where she was because she didn't settle for less; she studied and worked her ass off, and didn't let herself get too settled anywhere she was unfulfilled. And that instead of complaining, maybe I should ask myself what I'm feeling jealous of and what I need to do to get it. I told her she was missing the point; she'll always be around people who don't have what she does, and she could be a little more modest about it. She said I was the only one who seemed to have a problem with it, and stormed off... AITA for what I said?

While a religious community may provide a sense of belonging, moral guidance, and a shared set of values, a group of people you respect and share values with can indeed have a similar positive impact on individuals. This type of group, often referred to as a "secular community" or "values-based community," can provide a supportive environment that encourages personal growth and self-improvement. Here are some reasons why a values-based community can be just as effective as a religious community in pushing people to be better: 1. **Shared values and goals**: When you surround yourself with people who share your values and goals, you're more likely to feel motivated and inspired to work towards them. This shared sense of purpose can create a sense of accountability and encourage individuals to strive for personal growth. 2. **Supportive environment**: A values-based community can provide a safe and supportive space for individuals to discuss their challenges, share their experiences, and learn from one another. This environment can foster a sense of trust, empathy, and understanding, which can be just as powerful as the sense of community found in a religious setting. 3. **Role models and mentors**: When you surround yourself with people you respect and admire, you're more likely to be inspired by their examples and motivated to emulate their positive qualities. This can be especially true if you have a mentor or role model within the group who can offer guidance and support. 4. **Accountability and encouragement**: A values-based community can provide a sense of accountability, where individuals feel motivated to live up to the expectations of their peers. This can be a powerful driver of personal growth, as individuals strive to meet the standards set by their community. 5. **Flexibility and autonomy**: Unlike a religious community, a values-based community may offer more flexibility and autonomy, allowing individuals to explore their own spirituality and values without feeling bound by dogma or doctrine. However, it's worth noting that a values-based community may not provide the same level of structure and guidance as a religious community. Without a clear set of rules or teachings, individuals may need to take more responsibility for their own personal growth and development. Ultimately, whether a values-based community can push people to be better in the same way a religious community does depends on the specific individuals involved and the values they share. If you're part of a group that provides a supportive environment, shared values, and a sense of accountability, you may find that it has a similar positive impact on your personal growth and development.

prediction.raw:
I would say NTA (Not The Asshole). Here's why:

While it's great that your girlfriend has a wonderful job with great benefits and a good work-life balance, it's understandable that you feel frustrated when she constantly brags about her work perks. It's not that you're jealous of her job, but rather that you feel she's being insensitive to the fact that not everyone has the same opportunities or circumstances.

Your girlfriend's response, accusing you of being jealous and telling you to reflect on what you're feeling, doesn't address the issue at hand. She's not considering the impact her behavior has on you and others who may not have the same advantages.

It's not about being modest or bragging; it's about being considerate of others and not making them feel like they're missing out. By constantly talking about her work perks, she's creating a sense of FOMO (fear of missing out) and making you feel like you're not good enough.

You're not asking her to stop talking about her job entirely, but rather to be more mindful of how her words affect others. It's a reasonable request, and it's not unreasonable to expect her to be more considerate of your feelings.

In this situation, it's not about being the "asshole" for pointing out her behavior; it's about being a partner who cares about your feelings and wants to have a more balanced conversation.
